body_markdown:
## **TL;DR**


- Start with a vetted independent contractor agreement template or consulting agreement template that covers the work, payment, and termination. Reuse approved terms rather than drafting each agreement anew.
- Ask counsel to review worker classification, intellectual-property assignment, confidentiality, and governing law when the arrangement raises questions or departs from approved terms.
- To send a freelancer a contract, verify the signer’s details, set the signing order and expiration date, and schedule reminders. Correct errors before anyone signs, then collect the contractor’s signature and your countersignature.
- Save the fully signed agreement with its audit history in secure, searchable storage. Record renewal or termination dates so you can find the agreement and act on it later.


## **Why contractor agreements need a workflow, not just a template**


An independent contractor agreement template gives you a starting set of terms, but it cannot ensure the right person reviews and signs the final document. A practical workflow covers three phases. You prepare the agreement, send and execute it, then manage the signed record. Without those steps, a founder could have an approved draft but no countersigned copy to find later.


Your operations staff can fill in approved fields, verify the recipient, track signatures, and store the executed agreement. Counsel should handle legal decisions, including worker classification and changes to intellectual-property or confidentiality terms. Separating those responsibilities lets you repeat administrative steps without treating a reusable template as legal approval for every engagement.


## **Preparing the agreement**


Start with an independent contractor agreement template or consulting agreement template that counsel has vetted for the kind of work you are hiring for. If you do not have an approved version, ask counsel to review one before using it as your standard. Reusing approved language saves you from redrafting common terms for every contractor while preserving the decisions already made about those terms.


A reusable template should give each engagement a consistent structure without copying the last contractor’s details. Fill in the contractor’s name, the work they will perform, deliverables, rate, and payment schedule. Use approved options for the agreement’s duration and termination notice. A written scope helps both sides identify what the contractor has agreed to deliver, but you still need to check that it describes the current project.


Keep legal choices out of routine form-filling. Counsel should assess worker classification against the actual working relationship, since calling someone a contractor in the agreement does not settle their legal status. Ask counsel to approve intellectual-property assignment and confidentiality terms, particularly when the contractor will create code or handle sensitive information. Counsel should also review the jurisdiction and governing-law provisions rather than having an operations owner select them without guidance.


Control which parts of the template you can change without further review. Keep a current approved version, mark the fields you may complete, and route requests to change other clauses back to counsel. For example, you can enter an agreed hourly rate in an approved field, but a contractor’s request to retain ownership of their work calls for legal review before you send the agreement.


## **Sending the agreement to a contractor or freelancer**


Check the recipient details before sending the approved agreement. Match the contractor’s legal name and email address to the document. If you are contracting with a freelancer’s company, confirm who can sign on its behalf.


To send a freelancer a contract directly, you can email the approved agreement as an attachment and ask them to sign and return it. Keep track of the version you sent so you can confirm that the returned copy contains the same terms. Alternatively, enter the freelancer’s email in an electronic signing tool and send a signing link. A tracked send lets you check whether the agreement is still awaiting a signature without relying on an email thread.


Set the signing order before you send. If your company signs after the contractor, assign the contractor the first signature and the authorized company signer the second. Check any expiration date on the signing request so the link stays available long enough for review. Set reminders at reasonable intervals, and give the freelancer a contact for questions about the document.


Correct errors before anyone signs. If the freelancer spots a wrong rate, name, or start date, update the approved document and send a new version rather than asking them to sign the old one. Route changes to legal terms through the appropriate reviewer before resending. Once the freelancer signs, collect the company countersignature and confirm that both parties receive the fully executed copy.


## **Basic e-signature versus full contract workflow**


Basic e-signature tools help you send an agreement, collect signatures, and download the signed document. Some also support signing order, reminders, and a record of who signed. If you send a freelancer one approved agreement and can reliably manage the resulting file, those features may be enough.


A contract workflow covers decisions and records around the signature. You can route a proposed change for internal approval before sending it, reuse approved terms for the next contractor, and track whether the contractor and your company have both signed. Structured contract data, such as the end date and payment terms, lets you find and manage obligations without reopening every PDF.


For example,[Common Paper](https://commonpaper.com/) connects electronic signatures with reusable agreements, internal approvals, and structured data. Those tools can help you keep the executed agreement and its status tied to the process that produced it. They do not decide whether a contractor is correctly classified or whether custom intellectual-property terms protect your company. Counsel should review questions that require legal judgment.


## **Managing the signed agreement**


Once both parties have signed, save the completed agreement with its audit history. The audit history should show who signed, when they signed, and which version they signed. Keep the record in a location with access limited to people who need it, rather than relying on the founder’s inbox or a link in a signing email.


Make the agreement easy to find when someone needs to act on it. Record the contractor’s name, the project, the effective date, and the agreement’s status alongside the signed copy. If a founder needs the contract during a dispute, those details help them locate the executed version rather than an earlier draft. HR and finance may also need the agreed scope and payment terms without searching through email.


Track the dates that require follow-up. A contractor agreement may end on a fixed date, renew under its terms, or require advance notice to terminate. Record the relevant dates and assign someone to check them before a deadline passes. File storage preserves the document, while ongoing contract management adds status tracking and structured data that you can use in other systems. Common Paper connects signed agreements with structured contract data and contract management, but you still need to decide which obligations to track and who owns them.


## **When to involve legal counsel**


Ask legal counsel to review the agreement before sending it if any of these conditions apply. Note that this is not an exhaustive list of situations when legal counsel is needed, but rather some of the most common ones.


- The contractor’s role or working arrangement raises questions about whether they should be classified as an employee. An agreement cannot settle classification by calling someone a contractor.
- The project needs custom intellectual-property terms, including terms for work that uses materials the contractor created earlier.
- The contractor will handle sensitive information that the approved confidentiality terms do not adequately cover.
- The contractor works in a jurisdiction the approved template does not cover.
- Anyone changes the approved template or proposes terms outside your standard options.


You can use contract software to route the draft for approval, track signatures, and store the executed agreement. Counsel must make the legal judgments behind classification and contract terms.


## **FAQs**


**Where do I get an independent contractor agreement template?** Ask your lawyer for a previously approved template, or have counsel review an independent contractor agreement template before you reuse it. Fill in the project scope, payment, and dates for each engagement. Have counsel review questions about worker classification, intellectual property, confidentiality, or governing law rather than resolving them by editing boilerplate.


**What’s the difference between an independent contractor agreement and a consulting agreement?** Both can govern work performed by someone outside your company. A consulting agreement template often describes advisory or specialized services, while an independent contractor agreement may cover a wider range of work. The document’s title does not determine whether the worker qualifies as an independent contractor. The working relationship and applicable law matter.


**Can I send a contract directly to a freelancer without a lawyer?** Yes, if you use approved terms and the engagement raises no new legal questions. Confirm the freelancer’s name and email address, identify the authorized signer for each side, and send the agreement for signature. Set an expiration date and reminders if your signing tool supports them. Ask counsel to review any change to approved terms or uncertainty about classification.


**What should I do if I need to correct a contract after sending it but before signature?** Withdraw or void the unsigned version, make the correction, and send a new copy. Tell the freelancer which version to sign so they do not use an outdated link or attachment. If either party has already signed, ask counsel whether the correction requires a new agreement or an amendment.


**How long should I keep a signed contractor agreement on file?** Keep the fully countersigned agreement and its signing history for the period required by applicable law and your record-retention policy. Retention rules vary, so ask counsel or your accountant to set a period rather than assuming one number fits every contract. Store the record securely and make it searchable by contractor name, project, and termination date.


## **Key takeaway**


For lean operations teams hiring more contractors, legal review needs a dependable process behind it. Use a vetted template, check who receives and signs each agreement, and keep the executed copy where you can find it. Those steps help prevent lost agreements and missed renewals. Ask counsel to assess worker classification before work begins, since a well-kept agreement cannot correct a misclassified role.
